title: Masked Differential-linear Distinguishers and Quantum Approaches
authors: Shobhit Pandey, Sarbani Sen, Debajyoti Bera, Ravi Anand
abstract: We introduce masked auto-correlation, a new primitive for the cryptanalysis of symmetric-key primitives, together with a quantum attack pipeline built on it. For a permutation $f$, output masks $α,β$, and an input difference $w$, masked auto-correlation (MAC) measures the correlation between the masked outputs $α\cdot f(x)$ and $β\cdot f(x\oplus w)$. The associated masked differential-linear (MDL) approximations strictly generalize several classical techniques; ordinary linear cryptanalysis, differential-linear cryptanalysis, and the differential-linear connectivity table all arise as special cases. Our central object of study is the problem of finding mask pairs with large masked cross-correlation -- those that yield powerful distinguishers -- which we call MAC Fishing. We give a constant-query quantum algorithm that samples such pairs according to their squared correlation, and we prove an exponential classical lower bound of $Ω(N/\log N)$ queries, by adapting the hardness of Fourier Fishing. To our knowledge this is the first result pairing a quantum upper bound with a classical lower bound for the core task of identifying high-correlation approximations, making quantum algorithms an absolute necessity. Building on this, we analyse the distribution of masked auto-correlation for random permutations, and then construct capacity-based distinguishers and key-recovery attacks, both classically and with a quadratic quantum speed-up using amplitude estimation. We validate our claims with experiments on reduced-round mini-AES.
summary: This paper introduces Masked Differential-linear (MDL) approximations for cryptanalysis, centered on the Masked Auto-correlation (MAC) primitive. It presents a quantum algorithm to efficiently find powerful distinguishing mask pairs, simultaneously proving a super-polynomial classical lower bound for this task. This work establishes a quantum necessity result for identifying strong statistical correlations in cryptographic systems.
main_problem: The paper develops a new framework, Masked Differential-linear (MDL) approximations, to cryptanalyze symmetric-key primitives by finding powerful statistical correlations.
main_result: It establishes the first result pairing a quantum upper bound with a classical lower bound for identifying high-correlation approximations, proving that quantum algorithms are necessary for this task.
method: The authors introduce Masked Auto-correlation (MAC) and use quantum algorithms (constant-query sampling) to find mask pairs with high cross-correlation, contrasting this with a proven classical lower bound.
model_or_system: The analysis is applied to the cryptanalysis of symmetric-key primitives, such as block ciphers (Mini-AES) and stream ciphers, using the permutation function $f$ as the core model.
key_observables: Masked cross-correlation $C_w^f(\alpha,  eta)$, capacity of the masked auto-correlation space, and the signed score $	ext{Score}(k)$ for key recovery.
important_parameters: The query complexity bounds ($\Omega(N/\log N)$ classically) and the quantum speed-up factor (quadratic speed-up via amplitude estimation).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that the quantum upper bound and classical lower bound establish an absolute necessity for quantum computation in this specific cryptanalytic task.
figures_summary: Figures compare the energy profile versus the sharply peaked signed score for key recovery, and show the success of the distinguishing capacity against random permutations.
paper_structure: The paper introduces MAC and MDL approximations, presents the quantum sampling algorithm and the classical lower bound (MAC Fishing), and then applies this pipeline to demonstrate both distinguishing and key-recovery attacks on Mini-AES and a Simon cipher.
why_interesting: While focused on cryptography, the rigorous development of quantum lower bounds and the explicit comparison between quantum and classical computational complexity for a core mathematical problem (finding high-correlation structures) is highly relevant to quantum information theory.

A total of 512 keys were randomly selected, sufficient number of mask pairs were sampled and the proportion of good pairs esti- mated to 0.95 confidence (using Wilson score). τ was set to 9/216. The values of w that were chosen were 0x0003 (top-left), 0x3009 (top-right), 0x0845 (bottom-left), 0x2504 (bottom-right).

Fig. 2. Variation in the values of MAC of sample (α, β, w) triplets across 50 random keys for 16-bit mini-AES. The root-mean-square (RMS) of the MAC values, across all keys, and with 95% confidence (Wilson’s score), are shown for all triplets.

The 16- dimensional multidimensional approximation was chosen earlier by identifying good mask pairs across a set of randomly chosen keys.
